matches.rationale: No finding identifies the unrealistically large and suspiciously consistent navigation success improvements (~5% on R2R‑CE, >13% on REVERIE‑CE) or the lack of associated trade‑offs in other metrics. The abstract‑table comparisons and statistical concerns in other tables do not capture the integrity issue with the reported SR gains in Tables 1 and 2.

The ground truth concerns a logical inconsistency between the Merging Discriminator update and Frustum Culling, making cross‑view patch tracking ambiguous. None of the findings address this specific logical flaw; the noted notation and dimensionality issues in the same section are distinct technical problems.

The corruption is an exaggerated novelty claim in the Introduction that understates prior work on dynamic scene updates and semantic alignment. No finding points to this specific argument or the overstated contrast with previous methods; the closest is about missing comparisons in Section 2, not the Introduction’s presentation distortion.

Prediction 4 directly addresses the same experiments (pre‑exploration and lifelong memory, Table 3) and the same issue: the paper does not disclose whether test scenes overlap with training scenes, raising concerns about data leakage and memorization, exactly matching the ground truth’s omission.

Prediction 6 identifies the missing ethical approvals, participant consent, and safety protocols in the real‑world robot experiments of Section 4.3 (Tables 4, 5), which is precisely the ethical omission described in the ground truth.

The abstract’s overconfident rhetoric (‘sets new state‑of‑the‑art’, ‘validates … practical deployment’) is not identified by any finding; the verifier’s abstract‑related note concerns missing baselines and the claim of ‘competitive performance’, which is a different issue.

The Related Work corruption is a failure to acknowledge concurrent works with similar hierarchical spatial representations, making the novelty claim overly unique. Prediction 9 mentions an acknowledged lack of comparative assessment but does not capture the core issue of ignoring specific prior works.

No finding addresses the conclusion’s inflated claims of state‑of‑the‑art and strong generalization that contradict the more cautious experimental results. All predictions concern other sections, so this inconsistency is not detected.

The noise‑robustness experiments in Section 4.6 are criticized for lacking targeted ablations on 3D representation degradation. No finding identifies this gap; the verifier did not raise any issues related to the design of the noise tests or the missing analysis of 3D representation quality.

The appendix omission of ethical statements for 3D scan and language annotation data is not covered by any finding. The only ethics‑related finding concerns real‑world robot experiments, not dataset privacy and consent in training data collection.

The claim about balancing real‑time adaptability and long‑term memory lacks supporting metrics on memory saturation or latency, but no finding points to this unsupported claim. The verifier’s comments on methodology do not capture this specific overstatement.

The Introduction’s use of absolutist language (‘achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance’) without caveats is not highlighted by any finding. No prediction targets the rhetorical framing of contributions in Section 1.
